newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila prepares for oil deregulation amid protests.
newsitem.headline: Manila prepares for oil deregulation amid protests.

text.p: The Philippines prepared on Friday to allow its domestic oil industry to function free of government control amid accusations the move will lead to a sharp increase in prices of petroleum products.
From Saturday, the local oil industry will be completely deregulated. But the country's three main refiners have given repeated assurances that prices will not be jacked up.

"The oil industry will now be free to determine petroleum prices," said Bayani Faylona, chairman of the Energy Regulatory Board (ERB), the body that has set petroleum prices during the last 25 years that the local oil industry has been under government control.
"But as far as I know, the oil companies are not going to make any drastic changes."
"They would like to show the public that they are not going to take advantage of full deregulation by increasing prices unreasonably," Faylona added.
He also said that before regulation began in the early 1970s, Philippine petroleum prices were among the world's lowest.
Pilipinas Shell Petroleum Corp president Reinier Willems told Reuters earlier this week that there would likely be no drastic changes in local pump prices.

In the medium and long-term, however, Willems said there would likely be price wars among industry players and more intense competition. Petron Corp and Caltex Philippines Inc are the two other main refiners in the country.
But critics have strengthened their opposition to the deregulation programme.

Four opposition congressmen along with three human rights groups filed a petition with the Supreme Court on Thursday to halt the move. The court has yet to make a decision on whether to issue a temporary restraining order.

One group, the Bagong Alyansang Makabayan (Bayan) or the New Patriotic Alliance, started a two-day protest rally in front of the offices of the three oil companies in Manila's financial district of Makati on Friday. A night vigil and march near the presidential palace would also be held.

"Our opposition to oil deregulation is unequivocal. This will only lead to cartelisation and even if they claim that new entrants will guard against cartels, these minor players will not be a match for the established oil companies," Nathanael Santiago, a Bayan official, told Reuters.
The government has taken the criticism in its stride.
"When we were regulating they were complaining every time we fixed prices. Now that we are deregulating, they are also complaining, what can I say?" Faylona said.
Big business has voiced its support for full deregulation.

Raul Concepcion, president of the Federation of Philippine Industries, said that based on his group's calculations, increases once full deregulation set in would have a minimal effect on prices of basic commodities.
Meanwhile, the three oil companies were carefully watching each other's moves in adjusting prices.
Petron Corp started the ball rolling with an announcement late on Thursday that it would reduce its wholesale posted price by an average of one centavo per litre effective on Saturday.

"We are looking at Petron before we make our own adjustments. We were earlier planning to raise prices by an average of five to six centavos but with Petron's announcement, we may just lower (prices) ..." a source at Caltex told Reuters.
